sections.title: The five parts of the machine
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: What a Programmer's Model Is
Slide 2: One Model, Many Instances
Slide 15: What Changed, Coming From 8 Bits
Slide 16: The Programmer's Model, Complete
Slide 17: What You Should Be Able to Say
sections.body:
A **programmer’s model** defines software-visible **state** (stored values) and read/write behavior. Transistors, pipelines and wiring are hidden implementation details. A **bus** carries addresses and data between blocks.

Five parts organize this model: **CPU registers** (working stores), **address space** (usable addresses), **peripheral registers** (device controls), execution modes/stacks, and exceptions. A **stack** saves values for later; an **exception** runs a handler instead of ordinary code. Vendors may rename these parts.

**Architecture** is the CPU’s software contract. **xPSR** stores result flags, execution state and exception identity; **NVIC** selects eligible interrupt handlers.

There are 16 CPU registers plus xPSR; other state uses memory-map addresses. Peripheral registers provide control, status and data. Thread/Handler mode distinguishes ordinary/exception code. Vectors store targets; NVIC selects requests.

If you know AVR, compare one feature at a time:

1. Working values: AVR has 32 × 8-bit registers; Cortex-M has 16 × 32-bit registers.
2. Device access: AVR IN/OUT use an I/O instruction space; Cortex-M uses ordinary loads/stores to device addresses.
3. Flash constants: AVR’s Harvard arrangement needs LPM/PROGMEM; Cortex-M’s unified software map permits ordinary pointer access.
4. Interrupt targets: AVR vector slots contain jumps; Cortex-M slots contain addresses.

Because a normal pointer can select a device, a wrong pointer can reach hardware.

sections.title: CPU state and special registers
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: Visible State, Part One — the Registers
Slide 3b: Every Core Register on One Page
sections.body:
**Operands** are operation inputs. CPU **registers** hold working values; the **ALU** (arithmetic and logic unit) calculates with them.

Operand organizations:

1. An **accumulator** reuses one main register for inputs/results: 6502/8051. Other state exists; this does not mean only one register.
2. An **operand stack** takes inputs from a last-in, first-out collection and puts results on top: JVM/Forth. This differs from a return-address memory stack.
3. A **register machine** names several working stores. ATmega128: 32 × 8-bit registers. Cortex-M: 16 × 32-bit, including 13 general-purpose and three stack/return/instruction registers.
4. x86-64: 16 × 64-bit. The 32-bit RISC-V example: 32 × 32-bit, including one always-zero register. These are comparisons, not additional programming targets.

**Spilling** saves register temporaries in memory. More registers need more encoding bits and context-save space. A **flag** records a result condition; **AAPCS** defines how function calls share registers.

**SP** is stack pointer; **LR**, return target; **PC**, instruction position. **MSP/PSP** are main/process stack pointers. Arguments enter functions; results leave them; scratch values may be overwritten. APSR/EPSR/IPSR view xPSR fields. N/Z/C/V mean negative/zero/carry/signed overflow; Thumb is the instruction set. Bits 5:0 includes bits 5 through 0.

| State | Purpose / bit positions |
|---|---|
| R0–R3 | Arguments, results, scratch |
| R4–R12 | General working values; R12 is scratch in AAPCS |
| R13 / SP | Selected stack pointer: MSP or PSP |
| R14 / LR | Saved return target |
| R15 / PC | Instruction position; writing PC branches |
| xPSR | Combined flags, execution state, exception identity |
| APSR view | N bit 31, Z 30, C 29, V 28 |
| EPSR view | Thumb T bit 24, always 1 for valid execution here |
| IPSR view | Exception number bits 5:0; 0 in Thread mode |
| PRIMASK | Bit 0 masks configurable interrupts when 1 |
| CONTROL | SPSEL bit 1; nPRIV bit 0 |

A **special core register** has no R number or normal memory address: MRS reads it; MSR writes it. ARMv6-M lacks BASEPRI/FAULTMASK, which M3/M4 add. Load, calculate in registers, then store; debuggers and crash frames expose working values.

sections.title: Addresses, alignment and byte order
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: Visible State, Part Two — One Flat Address Space
Slide 10: The Data Model — Width, Alignment, Byte Order
sections.body:
**I/O** means device input/output. **Memory-mapped I/O** uses ordinary loads/stores; **port-mapped I/O** uses separate addresses/instructions. x86 IN/OUT use 64 K ports; AVR also has I/O space. This Cortex-M uses memory-mapped I/O only.

**Flash** stores instructions/constants; **SRAM** stores changing values. **Alignment** is an appropriate multi-byte address boundary; **endianness** is byte order, without changing the number.

**Harvard** separates code/data spaces: AVR needs LPM/PROGMEM for Flash constants. The unified **von Neumann** software map permits ordinary loads from Flash/RAM, even with separate internal buses.

| Region | Address / contents |
|---|---|
| Code alias | 0x00000000; flash appears here at reset |
| Physical flash | 0x08000000 |
| SRAM | 0x20000000; variables, heap, stacks |
| Vendor peripherals | 0x40000000 region |
| Private peripheral region | 0xE0000000; ARM core devices |

A word is 32 bits. Narrow storage saves RAM but may need extra masking, so 8-bit computation is not inherently faster. An n-byte access needs an address divisible by n: words by 4, halfwords by 2. M0+ faults on unsupported unaligned access; ordinary M3/M4 accesses may work more slowly. Arbitrary byte-buffer casts to uint32_t* are unsafe.

STM32 is **little-endian**: 0x12345678 occupies increasing addresses as 78, 56, 34, 12. **Big-endian** reverses them; network byte order uses it, hence htonl conversions. ARM designs can support either.

sections.title: Peripheral roles and the correct manual
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: Visible State, Part Three — a Register Is Not a Variable
Slide 6: Every Peripheral Has the Same Three Registers
Slide 7: Two Kinds of Peripheral, Two Manuals
sections.body:
A **peripheral** is hardware such as a timer/serial port; registers control its changing **state machine**. Reads can clear flags or consume bytes; writes can drive pins or start conversions. **volatile** preserves required accesses, without locking other contexts.

Register roles: control chooses behavior, status reports progress, data transfers **payload** (useful data). USART sends/receives serial bytes; SPI is clocked serial; ADC converts voltage; GPIO reads/drives pins.

| Device | Control examples | Status | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| USART | CR1: enable, interrupts, format; baud divisor elsewhere | ISR | TDR / RDR |
| SPI | CR1: speed/polarity | SR | DR |
| ADC | CFGR: channel/resolution setup | ISR | DR |
| Timer | CR1, PSC, ARR | SR | CNT, CCR |
| GPIO | MODER, PUPDR | IDR | ODR, BSRR |

A device can have many registers within these three roles.

ARM supplies NVIC/SysTick/SCB in core_cm0plus.h; MPU is optional. ST supplies GPIO/USART/TIM/ADC/RCC in stm32c031xx.h. Use ARM’s guide for core behavior and ST’s manual/datasheet for gates/pins. An architectural option need not exist on this part.

Storing to GPIOA ODR at 0x50000014 can drive a pin: an ordinary memory instruction has a physical effect.

sections.title: Modes, stacks and exception vectors
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Visible State, Part Four — Modes and Stacks
Slide 9: Visible State, Part Five — the Exception Model
sections.body:
**Privilege** permits restricted operations. An **MMU** translates virtual addresses and protects desktop processes; this MCU has none. An optional **MPU** checks permissions without virtual maps. A stray pointer can corrupt RAM, operate hardware or fault.

**Thread mode** runs ordinary code; **Handler mode** runs exceptions. **MSP/PSP** mean main/process stack pointers. An **RTOS** schedules tasks; a **vector** stores an indexed exception target.

Thread mode may use MSP/PSP. Handlers are always privileged and use MSP. CONTROL resets to 0: SPSEL=0 chooses MSP, nPRIV=0 privilege. An RTOS may select PSP and lower Thread privilege.

**Non-vectored interrupts** enter a source dispatcher; **vectored interrupts** use a table. AVR slots hold jumps, x86 descriptors, Cortex-M addresses. Entry 0 is initial SP; 1 is Reset_Handler; IRQ n uses 16+n. USART2 IRQ 28 uses entry 44 and IPSR=44 (0x2C); its handler must appear in the table, without runtime registration.

USART2’s table base is 0x08000000; its full 32-bit IPSR read is 0x0000002C. Only CONTROL’s defined low fields are implemented; other bits are reserved.

sections.title: Clock gates, pin ownership and implementation costs
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Your Responsibilities — Two Gates You Must Open
Slide 12: Your Responsibilities — the Clock Is Yours Too
Slide 13: Where the Implementation Leaks Through
Slide 14: The Implementation, Once
sections.body:
**RCC** (reset and clock control) enables peripheral pulses through a **clock gate**. Without the gate, writes may be ignored and reads return zero. Then select the pin’s owner with its **mux** (multiplexer); a wrong owner disconnects working hardware from the pin.

An **oscillator** generates pulses; a **prescaler** divides frequency. **Baud** is serial symbols/s; a divisor derives it from the actual device clock. MHz means million cycles/s.

The 48 MHz oscillator feeds separate core/bus prescalers. UART needs its actual clock and correct pin owner. Millisecond delays require known tick timing.

Three implementation details still matter to software:

1. A pipeline overlaps instruction stages. This affects the PC used for relative addressing and the cost of branches.
2. Separate AHB/APB buses carry accesses to different blocks. Choose the correct RCC gate register, such as AHBENR or APBENR1.
3. Flash can respond more slowly than the CPU. FLASH->ACR configures wait states: allow enough response time before increasing frequency, then poll readiness. When reducing frequency, reduce wait states afterward.

The bus matrix connects SRAM, Flash, GPIO/DMA/RCC and the APB bridge to UART/SPI/I2C/timers/ADC; pins follow the mux. Large machines use caches for memory-speed gaps; this chip uses wait states and **prefetch** (early instruction fetch).

For 115200 baud, store the calculated divisor, not 115200 itself.

sections.title: Reading Thumb code and recognizing its limits
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: You Will Not Write Assembly. You Will Read It.
Slide 2: Thumb — the Only Instruction Set This Chip Has
Slide 3: The Good News — There Is Not Much to Learn
Slide 16: Thumb-1 and Thumb-2 — Two Generations
Slide 17: Which Thumb This Is — "Thumb-1, Plus Six"
sections.body:
**Disassembly** decodes instructions/operands to explain source gaps, writes, slow loops and optimization. **Optimization** changes instructions while preserving required behavior. Measurements below describe _spike/c031c6/Main.elf built with arm-none-eabi-gcc -Os (small-code optimization), not every program.

An **instruction set** defines decodable operations; an **encoding** is one instruction’s bits, whose width can differ from register width. **Code density** measures storage. Halfword=16 bits; mnemonic=instruction name; immediate=embedded number. FPU means floating-point unit; DSP means signal-processing operations.

**A32** is ARM’s 32-bit instruction state, begun in 1985. **Thumb** began in 1994 with ARM7TDMI: common 16-bit forms plus selected 32-bit extensions. It often saves ~30% code; the four-instruction example uses 10 rather than 16 bytes. Cortex-A/R switch states; Cortex-M is Thumb-only.

Compact encodings save bytes but complicate decoding: x86 uses 1–15 bytes; Thumb/MIPS16/RISC-V C compress common cases.

thumb/v6-m/nofp/libgcc.a means Thumb, ARMv6-M, no FPU. The image has 2100 instructions and 51 mnemonics, with this static composition:

| Instruction/group | Share |
|---|---:|
| MOVS | 15.9% |
| LDR | 15.3% |
| CMP | 8.3% |
| STR | 8.0% |
| ADDS | 5.7% |
| BL | 4.3% |
| LSLS | 4.0% |
| B | 3.9% |
| BNE | 3.6% |
| BEQ | 3.5% |
| SUBS | 2.5% |
| PUSH/POP | 4.6% |

PUSH/POP count as two mnemonics: these thirteen cover 79.6% of stored instructions, not runtime CPU time.

Thumb-2 arrived in 2003 with ARMv6T2. It mixes narrow and wide forms in one instruction stream. Top halfword bits 11101/11110/11111 indicate that another halfword follows.

Compare capabilities in stages:

1. M0/M0+ uses Thumb-1 plus six wide instructions: BL, MRS, MSR, DSB, DMB, ISB. Most forms use R0–R7 and update flags.
2. M3 (ARMv7-M) provides full Thumb-2: SDIV/UDIV hardware division, IT conditional blocks of up to four instructions, wider register/immediate choices, MOVW/MOVT constant construction and larger offsets. M3 has no FPU.
3. M4/M7 (ARMv7E-M) add DSP operations. M4F/M7 variants may provide floating-point hardware.

Narrow immediates are usually 0–255; larger cores offer 12-bit modified constants. The .n suffix means 16-bit narrow; .w means 32-bit wide. An instruction supported by M4 is not automatically supported by M0+.

BL at 0x0800028A encodes F7FF FFCF; next PC 0x0800028E plus signed displacement -98 reaches 0x0800022C. Its fields are opcode 31:27, S 26, imm10 25:16, J1 13, J2 11, imm11 10:0; reconstructed displacement S:I1:I2:imm10:imm11:0. Ordinary narrow unconditional branches reach about ±2 KB; calls require a wide encoding.

Cumulative shares: 15.9, 31.2, 39.5, 47.5, 53.2, 57.5, 61.5, 65.4, 69.0, 72.5, 75.0, 79.6%; remaining 38 mnemonics cover the rest. A32 supports predicates; this narrow Thumb subset uses conditional branches.

sections.title: Loads, arithmetic, bit fields and conditions
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: Load / Store — Two Machine Models, and Which One This Is
Slide 5: Arithmetic and Logic
Slide 6: Shifts — Why `lsls` Is 4% of All Code
Slide 7: Flags and Conditional Branches
sections.body:
A **load** copies memory to a register; a **store** copies back. **Load–store** arithmetic uses registers: counter++ becomes LDR/ADDS/STR on ARM/RISC-V/MIPS/AVR. **Register–memory** x86/68000/S360 can combine arithmetic and memory operands; both still read/write memory once. AVR SBI operates selected I/O bits. M0+ has no equivalent; STM32 BSRR changes pins in one atomic store (no partly observed command).

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| LDR / STR | 32-bit load/store |
| LDRB / STRB | Byte transfer |
| LDRH / STRH | Halfword transfer |
| LDRSH | Sign-extended 16-bit load |
| MOVS | Immediate or register copy; no memory access |
| ADDS / SUBS / NEGS | Add, subtract, 0 minus operand |
| MULS | Multiply and keep low 32 bits |
| ADCS | Add with carry; useful for multiword sums |
| ANDS / ORRS / EORS | Bit AND / OR / XOR |
| BICS | AND with inverted mask; x &= ~mask |
| LSLS / LSRS | Left shift / unsigned right shift |
| ASRS / RORS | Sign-preserving right shift / rotate right |

A **mask** selects bits; a **shift** moves them. **Sign extension** repeats the sign into added upper bits. **Carry** is an extra unsigned result bit; **signed overflow** means the result exceeds signed width.

M0+ a/b calls __aeabi_uidiv; the sample map includes _udivsi3.o at 0x080000B4 because C division required it. Most narrow arithmetic updates flags automatically, hence S suffixes. GPIO bit-field shifts such as 2u << (pin*2) explain frequent LSLS. ASRS preserves negative signs; logical shifts fill zeros. For signed negative numbers, arithmetic shift rounds differently from C division that truncates toward zero.

CMP subtracts without retaining its result; TST similarly tests an AND. APSR N31/Z30/C29/V28 records negative/zero/carry-or-no-borrow/signed overflow. BEQ uses Z=1; BNE Z=0; BLT/BGE use signed N versus V; BCC/BCS use unsigned carry; BMI/BPL use N. Flags let one comparison feed multiple branches but create hidden dependencies; RISC-V compare-and-branch (e.g. blt a 0, a 1, L) avoids that state.

Worked operations: LSLS by 3 multiplies an unsigned value by 8 when no significant bits are discarded; LSRS by 3 divides unsigned values by 8. GPIOA->MODER uses shifted fields such as 2u << (pin*2). ADCS carries from a low 32-bit sum into the high word of a 64-bit sum.

sections.title: Calls, the ABI and tagged return addresses
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Branches, Calls and Returns
Slide 18: Who Owns Which Register — the Calling Convention
Slide 19: The Thumb Bit — an Odd Address That Is Not a Bug
Slide 20: `LR` Is Odd Too — Reading a Return Address
sections.body:
A **branch** changes the next instruction. B is direct; conditional B tests flags. BL calls by saving return target in **LR**, then branching; BX LR returns. PUSH saves registers, POP restores; POP PC also branches. Preserve LR before nested calls.

x86/68000/AVR save return addresses on memory stacks; ARM/RISC-V/MIPS/PowerPC use link registers. A **leaf** makes no calls and may return directly in LR. A **non-leaf** preserves LR before another BL overwrites it.

**ABI** (application binary interface) defines machine-code conventions; **AAPCS** is ARM’s calling convention. **Caller-saved** values need protection before a call; **callee-saved** registers must be restored by the called function if used.

AAPCS lets separately compiled code agree. R0–R3 carry early arguments and R0 carries a simple result; R0–R3/R12 are caller-saved scratch. R4–R11 are callee-saved; SP has alignment/preservation rules, LR/PC are special. _write(fd, buf, len) receives R0, R1, R2 and returns len in R0. Its push {r4, r5, r6, r7, lr} protects the registers it uses and its return; pop {r4, r5, r6, r7, pc} combines restore and return.

Vector bytes 00 30 00 20 mean SP=0x20003000; 75 02 00 08 mean Reset_Handler target 0x08000275, while instructions begin at 0x08000274. Function target bit 0 is the Thumb-state tag, not an extra byte of code. Target bits 31:1 hold the address. Clearing the tag can fault on reset.

BL at 0x0800028A is four bytes, so next instruction is 0x0800028E. LR receives 0x0800028F. BX LR or POP PC consumes the tag and resumes at LR & ~1 = 0x0800028E. An even computed function target is suspect. During an exception LR can instead contain EXC_RETURN such as 0xFFFFFFF9 or 0xFFFFFFFD, which requests hardware unstacking rather than an ordinary code branch.

The sample NMI vector is 0x08000229 (bytes 29 02 00 08). Initial SP 0x20003000 is the top of the 12 KB SRAM allocation.

sections.title: Addresses, encodings and literal pools
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: How You Reach Memory — Addressing Modes
Slide 10: The Offsets Are Small, and You Can See When They Run Out
Slide 11: A Real Function, Disassembled
Slide 12: Where Do Big Constants Live?
Slide 13: A Polling Loop, in Four Instructions
sections.body:
An address is often **base+offset**: block start plus byte position. **CMSIS** (Common Microcontroller Software Interface Standard) field names compile to this arithmetic. Narrow Thumb is 16-bit: [r1]=*p; [r4,#28]=member; [r1,r3]=runtime byte index; [sp,#8]=local; [pc,#44]=constant. M3+ adds scaled indices and pre/post-updated bases.

| Narrow load | Immediate field | Byte reach |
|---|---|---|
| LDR base-relative | imm5 × 4 | 0–124 |
| LDRH | imm5 × 2 | 0–62 |
| LDRB | imm5 | 0–31 |
| LDR SP-relative | imm8 × 4 | 0–1020 |

Narrow offsets are positive; large/negative ones need M0+ base arithmetic. A retained field pointer may avoid it. M3+ supports positive 12-bit offsets through 4095 and other negative/indexed forms with separate limits.

Decode opcode, register fields, then scale the immediate. Rn=base, Rt=transferred register, Rd=destination; imm5/imm8=encoded five/eight-bit values. A **literal pool** stores nearby constants for loads.

Worked encodings:

1. 0x69E6 is LDR r6,[r4,#28]. 0x62A5 is STR r5,[r4,#40]. Both allocate bits 15:11 to the opcode, 10:6 to imm5, 5:3 to base Rn and 2:0 to transferred register Rt. Encoded offsets 7 and 10 are scaled by four, becoming 28 and 40 bytes.
2. MOVS r0,#7 is 0x2007: opcode at 15:11, Rd at 10:8 and imm8 at 7:0.
3. PC-relative LDR r2,#44 is 0x4A0B: Rt at 10:8 and imm8 at 7:0, again scaled by four.

SystemInit loads FLASH base 0x40022000, then LDR/BICS/ORRS/STR clears LATENCY bits 2:0 with mask 7 and inserts1. FLASH ACR also has DBG_SWEN bit 18, PROGEMPTY bit 16, ICRST bit 11, ICEN bit 9, PRFTEN bit 8. Arithmetic happens in registers; the update itself has one peripheral read and one write, not four peripheral bus accesses.

A 16-bit instruction cannot embed an arbitrary 32-bit address. Thumb uses a nearby literal pool; x86 lengthens its instruction; RISC-V uses LUI/ADDI; AArch64 MOVZ/MOVK. The sample pool contains FLASH 0x40022000, RCC 0x40021000, HSIDIV-clear mask 0xFFFFC7FF (zero bits 13:11), SystemCoreClock address 0x20000000 and 48000000=0x02DC6C00.

Polling FLASH latency compiles LDR, ANDS mask 7, CMP #1, BNE back to LDR. BNE 0xD1FB has opcode 15:12, condition 11:8 and signed imm8=0xFB=-5 halfwords. From PC+4=0x08000244 it branches -10 bytes to 0x0800023A. volatile makes each repeated LDR necessary.

Representative clock-update listing, with decoded instructions and addresses:
```asm
0800022c: 2007  movs r0, #7        @ latency field mask
0800022e: 2301  movs r3, #1        @ required wait-state count
08000230: 4a0b  ldr  r2, [pc, #44] @ FLASH register block address
08000232: 6811  ldr  r1, [r2, #0]  @ fetch FLASH->ACR
08000234: 4381  bics r1, r0        @ remove previous latency field
08000236: 430b  orrs r3, r1        @ insert new latency value
08000238: 6013  str  r3, [r2, #0]  @ publish register change
```
This implements `FLASH->ACR = (FLASH->ACR & ~FLASH_ACR_LATENCY) | FLASH_ACR_LATENCY_0`. The HSIDIV mask belongs to RCC->CR. Literal slots at 0x08000260, 0x08000264, 0x08000268, 0x0800026C and 0x08000270 contain the five pool words listed above. Narrow [r1,#-4] cannot be encoded. LDR r1,[r2,#0] is 0x6811; the combined call halfwords are 0xF7FFFFCF.

The polling loop encodings are 0x6813 (LDR), 0x4003 (ANDS), 0x2B01 (CMP) and 0xD1FB (BNE). Instruction addresses are 0x0800023A, 0x0800023C, 0x0800023E and 0x08000240. These raw values help connect debugger bytes to decoded operations.

sections.title: The build assigns real addresses
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: On a PC, an Operating System Hides All of This
Slide 2: Five Stages, Not One
Slide 3: The Compiler Sees One File at a Time
sections.body:
**Bare-metal** firmware supplies stack, globals and output setup before main, without OS startup services. gcc coordinates:

1. Preprocess: expand headers and macros.
2. Compile: translate C into assembly.
3. Assemble: encode instructions in an object file (.o).
4. Link: match definitions to references across separately compiled .c files.
5. Locate: use a linker script to assign fixed addresses.

A **symbol** names a function, object or linker address. Objects list definitions/unresolved references. Undefined reference=no definition; multiple definition=competing definitions. ST declares SystemCoreClock’s name/type; startup must allocate its definition if the vendor system file is absent.

**Address binding** chooses program addresses. A **relocatable image** accepts a loader-selected base; **virtual addresses** are translated to physical addresses by an MMU.

Binding occurs at build (fixed firmware/DOS .com), load (relocation), or execution (MMU). This chip has no loader/MMU: image addresses are fixed. Spike SystemInit=0x0800022C, SystemCoreClock=0x20000000. Desktop OSs hide these placement/startup jobs.

For contrast, MMU-separated desktop processes can both use virtual address 0x400000 without owning the same physical bytes.

sections.title: Sections and the memory budget
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: Your Program Is Not One Blob — It Is Sections
Slide 5: The Awkward One — `.data`
Slide 6: The Linker Script Is the Memory Map, Written Down
sections.body:
A **section** groups bytes with the same storage treatment. Flash holds .text, .rodata, vectors and .data initial values. SRAM holds writable .data, zero-initialized .bss, dynamic-allocation **heap**, and downward-growing **stack**. Startup copies .data and zeroes .bss; .bss needs no Flash zeros.

| Spike section | Bytes | Execution address |
|---|---:|---|
| .isr_vector |180|0x08000000|
| .text |4792|0x080000B4|
| .rodata |184|0x08002CAC|
| .data |96|0x20000000|
| .bss |364|0x20000060|

Linker **MEMORY** lists regions; **ORIGIN** is start, **LENGTH** capacity, rx read/execute, rw read/write. Alignment can add padding. These figures describe one build.

These are reported _spike/c031c6 build values, not universal locations. Linker MEMORY declares FLASH(rx) origin 0x08000000 length 32K and RAM(rw) origin 0x20000000 length 12K. The spike summary reports FLASH 5260 B/32768=16.05%, RAM 2000 B/12288=16.28%. Reservations/alignment mean totals need not equal only the listed data sections. A falsely large RAM length can permit a stack outside physical memory.

```c
src = &_sidata;
for (dst = &_sdata; dst < &_edata;) *dst++ = *src++;
for (dst = &_sbss; dst < &_ebss;) *dst++ = 0;
```
Linker symbols mark Flash source and SRAM .data/.bss bounds. Reset_Handler copies/clears before main. Missing .bss clearing makes values RAM-history-dependent. .bss 364 uses no Flash payload; .data96 uses 96 bytes in each memory.

The reset-clock definition `uint32_t SystemCoreClock = 12000000;` is a .data example: its initial 12 MHz value must be copied before SystemInit updates it.

sections.title: Firmware files, boot and observation
sourceHeadings: Slide 7: What Actually Gets Programmed
Slide 8: What Runs Before `main()`
Slide 9: Your Instruments
Slide 10: What You Should Be Able to Say
sections.body:
**ELF** holds addressed code, symbols and debug information; **BIN** holds raw Flash bytes; **Intel HEX** holds printable addressed records. Wokwi/Renode execute built Main.elf, not compile C. Wokwi exposes wiring/displays; Renode serial/registers/instructions. These free tools model selected behavior, not all silicon features.

HEX fields are byte count, low address, type, data, checksum. A **checksum** detects record damage, not correct vectors/code. Type 04 supplies upper address bits for later type 00 data.

The spike records are:
```
:020000040800F2
:1000000000300020750200082902000829020008BB
```
Colon starts a record. The second record has count 10 hex=16 bytes, offset 0000, type 00=data, ending checksumBB. Bytes 00300020 decode little-endian initial SP 0x20003000;75020008 decode reset target 0x08000275 (actual code 0x08000274 with Thumb tag);29020008 is NMI 0x08000229. Type 04 in the first record sets upper address bits to 0800, placing subsequent data at 0x08000000. A small AVR image fitting 16-bit addresses did not require that upper-address record.

At reset Flash aliases zero. Hardware loads SP=vector[0], reset target=vector[1]; software copies .data, clears .bss, runs SystemInit/__libc_init_array, then main. A PC instead starts firmware at a fixed reset location before bootloader/kernel/user program. Observe execution and pins: build/checksum alone proves neither.

sections.title: Polling, interrupts and DMA
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: Three Ways to Meet the Hardware
Slide 2: An Interrupt Is a Hardware-Forced Function Call
Slide 3: Now You Have Two Programs Sharing One Memory
sections.body:
**Polling** repeatedly reads status and occupies CPU; short waits may cost less than interrupts. An **interrupt** requests a handler while CPU works elsewhere. **DMA** (direct memory access) moves payload without CPU copying each byte, but needs setup and buffer ownership.

An **exception frame** saves interrupted registers. **ISR** means interrupt service routine/handler. Caller-clobbered registers may change in calls; callee-saved registers must be preserved. Hardware/compiler divide this work.

Entry occurs between instructions: hardware stacks R0–R3/R12/LR/PC/xPSR, eight 32-bit words=32 bytes, selects a vector and enters Handler mode. Return restores them. Hardware saves AAPCS caller-clobbered state; compiler saves used callee-saved registers. Exact handler names replace vector defaults.

xPSR carries N31/Z30/C29/V28, T24 and exception identity 5:0. PRIMASK bit 0 can suppress configurable interrupts. CONTROL bit 1 selects Thread MSP/PSP; bit 0 controls privilege; handlers always use MSP. main and handlers share memory even though each can interrupt the other’s sequence. This creates compiler visibility and interleaving problems that need different remedies.

The field names are PRIMASK.PM at bit 0, CONTROL.SPSEL at bit 1 and CONTROL.nPRIV at bit 0. SPSEL=0 selects MSP, 1 selects PSP in Thread mode; nPRIV=0 means privileged, 1 unprivileged. Handler mode stays privileged.

sections.title: Visibility, atomicity and tearing
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: Hazard One — the Compiler Does Not Believe You
Slide 5: Hazard Two — the Interrupt Lands Mid-Update
Slide 6: A Bug That Only Appears Sometimes
Slide 7: Not Everything Needs Protecting
sections.body:
The **as-if rule** permits cached ordinary-global reads while preserving required C behavior. Hardware/ISR changes may then go unnoticed. **volatile** preserves accesses, without mutual exclusion or an indivisible multi-instruction update.

```c
volatile uint32_t counter;
/* main and ISR both increment: unsafe even with volatile */
```
Main loads 5, adds 1, stores 6. An ISR between load/store can also load 5/store 6: two increments produce 6 instead of 7. A **race** depends on ordering; **mutual exclusion** prevents overlap; **atomic** means no observed partial operation.

A **critical section** protects the whole shared sequence. Preserve the incoming interrupt mask, block handlers, finish, then restore it; nested callers may already have interrupts blocked.

On single-core M0+, CMSIS disable/enable emits CPSID I/CPSIE I, changing PRIMASK bit 0. Preserve the old mask:```c
uint32_t saved = __get_PRIMASK();
__disable_irq();
counter++;
__set_PRIMASK(saved);
```
OS threads need synchronization, such as mutexes. Local interrupt masks cannot stop another core; use atomic/synchronization operations, e.g. larger ARM LDREX/STREX or x86 locked operations. M0+ lacks exclusive-access instructions.

| Sharing pattern | Risk |
|---|---|
| ISR alone writes aligned byte/word, main reads | Access itself is indivisible; volatile required |
| ISR sets, main clears flag | A newly arriving event can be lost; analyze protocol |
| Both increment | Read-modify-write race |
| Shared uint64_t on32-bit core | Two accesses can tear |
| Multi-field struct | Reader can combine unrelated generations |

**Tearing** combines old/new parts into an unpublished value; individually atomic fields do not guarantee a consistent pair. Keep masked regions short. Illustrative source estimates: two instructions at 48 MHz≈40 ns; symptoms ~7 hours at 1000 events/s or 40 minutes at 10000/s, depending on update rate/phase, not measured guarantees. Inventory each global’s users; long successful runs cannot rule out races.

sections.body:
**NVIC** (nested vectored interrupt controller) selects eligible requests. **Priority** means urgency; **preemption** interrupts less urgent work. Smaller numbers are more urgent. Top two bits per byte give levels 0–3. IPR[0]: IRQ 0 bits 7:6, IRQ 1 15:14, IRQ 2 23:22, IRQ 3 31:30. ISR-shared data still needs protection.

**Interrupt latency** is event-to-first-handler-instruction delay; masking/higher-priority work increases it. Equal/lower priorities wait: record fast evidence and process slowly in main. **Priority inversion** makes urgent work wait for a less urgent resource owner; Mars Pathfinder’s1997 resets illustrate it.

**Model → Map → Measure**: identify hardware role, find register fields, observe behavior. **Visibility** preserves accesses; **indivisibility** prevents observed partial operations. Sharing may require both.

Combine one address map, control/status/data, gates/muxes, load–modify–store, linker placement and startup. Practice lost-update traces, tearing predictions, polling/interrupt/DMA choices and priority fields.

CMSIS exposes these priority words as NVIC->IPR. IRQ priorities occupy bytes, even though each byte implements just its top two bits.

Nucleo-C031C6: 48 MHz Cortex-M0+, 32 KB Flash, 12 KB SRAM. A **header** is a connector row; PA5 names an MCU pin. ST morpho exposes pins; Arduino labels A0–A5/D0–D15 may duplicate them, e.g. PA5/D13.

PB0–PB7 LED **anodes** (+) connect to pins; cathodes to ground. PA5/LD4 is heartbeat. PA2 AF1=USART2 TX; PA3 AF1=RX, unused here. **AF** selects peripheral ownership. Wokwi’s duplicate PB0 is nucleo:PB0.1; use accepted wire names. Preserve PA13/PA14 **SWD** (serial wire debug).

| Region / block | Exact address |
|---|---|
| Flash32 KB |0x08000000–0x08007FFF; reset alias at 0|
| SRAM 12 KB |0x20000000–0x20002FFF; stack starts just above at 0x20003000|
| GPIOA / GPIOB |0x50000000 /0x50000400|
| RCC / FLASH |0x40021000 /0x40022000|
| USART2 |0x40004400|
| System control space |0xE000E000|
| SysTick |0xE000E010|

32-bit addresses span 4 GB, mostly unimplemented. C0 GPIO starts at 0x50000000, unlike F4; addressability is not installed memory.

**CMSIS** headers define register pointers, struct offsets and volatile members. -> selects a field. **HAL** is a separate driver library; CMSIS names require no linked driver.

GPIOA->ODR=0x50000000+0x14. In this -Os toggle comparison, named form used 14 bytes; raw 0x50000014 used 12 code+4 literal=16. Names add no runtime abstraction and may help optimization.

The lesson’s Wokwi capability list excludes DMA, RTC, IWDG, PWR, SYSCFG, DBG; SPI/I2C are master-only. C0 EXTI owns EXTICR, enabling pin interrupts without SYSCFG. Low-power behavior needs another instrument; neither simulator measures current. These are documented simulator limits at the source snapshot, not silicon limits.

The unified map spans 0x00000000–0xFFFFFFFF; ordinary vendor peripherals start in the 0x40000000 region. `GPIOA->MODER` and `GPIOA->IDR` are struct fields, while `GPIOB->MODER` configures and `GPIOB->ODR` drives the bar. `GPIOA->AFR[0]` is at 0x50000020. On C0 use `EXTI->EXTICR[]`; on F4 the equivalent is `SYSCFG->EXTICR[]`.

sections.body:
**RCC** (reset and clock control), base 0x40021000, gates peripheral pulses. Enable the right gate first. Reset registers restart blocks; sleep gates control sleep clocks. Oscillators generate pulses; dividers reduce rate. Offsets below are hexadecimal bytes.

| Offset | Register | Role |
|---|---|---|
|00|CR|Oscillator control/divisions/readiness|
|04|ICSCR|Factory HSI trimming|
|08|CFGR|Clock-source selection, bus divisions, MCO|
|18/1C/20|CIER/CIFR/CICR|Clock interrupt enable/flag/clear|
|24/28/2C/30|IOPRSTR/AHBRSTR/APBRSTR1/APBRSTR2|Peripheral reset|
|34|IOPENR|GPIO gates|
|38|AHBENR|DMA, flash, CRC gates|
|3C|APBENR1|TIM3, USART2, I2C1, PWR and other gates|
|40|APBENR2|TIM1, SPI1, USART1, ADC gates|
|44/48/4C/50|IOPSMENR/AHBSMENR/APBSMENR1/APBSMENR2|Sleep-mode gates|
|54|CCIPR|Peripheral kernel-clock selection|
|5C/60|CSR1/CSR2|Low-speed oscillators/reset-cause state|

Start with GPIOA/B in IOPENR and USART2 in APBENR1. Other fields cover oscillator control/readiness and feature-specific gates.

CR fields: CSSON bit 19, HSEBYP bit 18, HSERDY bit 17, HSEON bit 16, HSIDIV bits 13:11, HSIRDY bit 10, HSIKERON bit 9, HSION bit 8, HSIKERDIV bits 7:5. IOPENR gives A0, B1, C2, D3, F5. APBENR1 includes TIM3EN1, RTCAPBEN bit 10, WWDGEN bit 11, USART2EN17, I2C1EN21, DBGEN bit 27, PWREN bit 28.

Enable GPIOA/B bits 0/1 at 0x40021034 and USART2 bit 17 at 0x4002103C before setup. Unclocked writes can vanish. Source addresses were checked against ST CMSIS using compile-time assertions.

Use exact CMSIS expressions `RCC->IOPENR |= RCC_IOPENR_GPIOAEN | RCC_IOPENR_GPIOBEN;` and `RCC->APBENR1 |= RCC_APBENR1_USART2EN;` for these gates.

sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output; A/B layouts match, bases 0x400 apart. **Mode** selects input/output/peripheral/analog; analog disables digital input. **AFR** selects the peripheral. A **field** groups setting bits; a **nibble** is four bits. **Slew** is transition speed; pulls bias undriven inputs. **Push-pull** drives high/low; **open-drain** drives low or releases to a pull-up.

| Offset | GPIO register | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
|00|MODER|2 bits/pin:00input, 01output, 10alternate, 11analog|
|04|OTYPER|1bit/pin push-pull/open-drain|
|08|OSPEEDR|2 bits/pin edge slew|
|0C|PUPDR|2 bits/pin pulls|
|10|IDR|Actual pin level|
|14|ODR|Requested output; toggle PA5/pattern PB0–7|
|18|BSRR|Atomic set/reset commands|
|1C|LCKR|Lock configuration|
|20/24|AFR[0]/[1]|4 bits/pin peripheral selection for 0–7/8–15|
|28|BRR|Reset commands|

Pin n uses MODER bits 2n+1:2n, ODR/IDR bitn, AFR nibble 4(n mod 8)+3:4(n mod 8). PA5 becomes output, PA2/PA3 alternate with AFR1. PB0–PB7 each use MODER 01 and ODR bits 7:0; upper pins are preserved. MODER 10 without the correct AFR choice is insufficient.

USART2 base 0x40004400:

| Offset | Register | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
|00|CR1|Enable, word length/parity, interrupts|
|04|CR2|Stop bits, swap/inversion|
|08|CR3|Flow control, DMA, error IRQ|
|0C|BRR|Baud divisor|
|10|GTPR|Smartcard guard/IrDA prescale|
|14|RTOR|Receive timeout|
|18|RQR|Flush/break requests|
|1C|ISR|Status|
|20|ICR|Write1 to clear flags|
|24|RDR|Received data|
|28|TDR|Transmit data|
|2C|PRESC|Kernel clock prescaler|

USART **UE/TE/RE** enable device/transmit/receive. **TXE_TXFNF** reports transmit room. **Baud** is symbols/s; BRR stores a clock divisor, not the baud number.

CR1 fields used/visible:UE0, RE2, TE3, RXNEIE bit 5, TXEIE bit 7, PCE bit 10, M0 12, OVER8 15, M1 28, FIFOEN bit 29. ISR includes FE1, ORE bit 3, RXNE_RXFNE bit 5, TC6, TXE_TXFNF bit 7, BUSY bit 16, TEACK bit 21. TDR payload field 8:0; BRR15:0. Rounded baud divisor=(48000000+57600)/115200=417=0x01A1. EnableUE/TE/RE, wait for TXE_TXFNF, then write TDR. The divisor is valid only for the actual selected UART clock.

sections.title: Reset vectors and weak handlers
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: `main()` Is Not Where Your Program Starts
Slide 2: The Two Files That Do It
Slide 5: Reset, in Hardware, Before Any Code
Slide 6: The Vector Table Is Just an Array at a Known Address
Slide 7: The First Eight Bytes of Your Own Firmware
Slide 8: Weak Aliases — and the Trap That Costs an Afternoon
sections.body:
link.ld places addresses; startup.c creates vectors and prepares C memory before main. A **vector table** starts with initial SP, then exception targets. Cortex-M loads SP/reset target before executing, permitting C Reset_Handler; AVR traditionally sets SP in assembly. A **weak handler** is an overridable default.

```c
__attribute__((section(".isr_vector"), used))
void (* const vectors[])(void) = {
    (void (*)(void))&_estack, Reset_Handler, NMI_Handler,
    HardFault_Handler, 0,0,0,0,0,0,0, SVC_Handler,
    0,0, PendSV_Handler, SysTick_Handler
    /* external IRQs follow */
};
```
Attributes: **section** names placement; **used** prevents compiler deletion; **weak** allows replacement; **alias** shares another function target. **Section garbage collection** removes unused linker sections, so vectors also need linker retention.

Vectors live at Flash base; const keeps them read-only. Entry 0 is a cast stack value, not callable code. Core entries 0–15 precede peripheral entries; this table uses 180 bytes.

This lesson’s HEX begins data00300020 0xC5060008 79060008 79060008, checksumBF. Little-endian words decode SP 0x20003000, reset 0x080006C5, NMI/HardFault 0x08000679. Actual Reset_Handler instructions begin 0x080006C4; bit 0 tags Thumb. The repeated NMI/HardFault address comes from weak aliases to Default_Handler.

```c
void TIM3_IRQHandler(void)
    __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
```
An exact ordinary definition overrides weak TIM3_IRQHandler. TIM3_IRQhandler’s case mismatch leaves the default installed and an unused function, without diagnostic. Check names/vector symbols for stalled interrupts.

RAM length 12 K is 0x3000 bytes, giving 0x20000000 + 0x3000 = 0x20003000. The source files are approximately 140 lines of startup and 70 lines of linker script; their size is not a hardware requirement.

A **startup witness** exposes initialization. Banner addresses come from linker symbols and can change on rebuild. This build expects: SystemCoreClock 48000000 Hz; vectors 0x08000000; Flash data0x08001D64; SRAM data0x20000000–0x20000064 (100 B); bss 0x20000064–0x200001D8 (372 B); heap 0x200001D8; stack 0x20003000; data_witness 0x00C0FFEE; zero witness 0.

Main.c patterns drive eight PB LEDs; PA5/LD4 toggles each frame; serial names patterns. Extend tables/timings/playlist. Predict each change, then record output:

| Lab change | Expected diagnostic consequence |
|---|---|
|Remove data copy|Nonzero initialized witness no longer guaranteed|
|Remove bss clear|Frame counter depends on previous RAM contents|
|Place vectors after text|May build/HEX-check cleanly but hardware consumes code bytes as SP/PC|
|Reduce RAM12K→8K→2K→1K|Stack top and reservations move; linker eventually reports overflow|

sourceHeadings: Slide 5: `MODER` — What Is This Pin?
Slide 6: A Pin Wakes Up Analog
Slide 7: `OTYPER` — How Does an Output Drive?
Slide 8: `OSPEEDR` — How Fast Do the Edges Change?
Slide 9: `PUPDR` — What Holds a Pin Nobody Drives?
Slide 10: `IDR` — Reading a Pin
Slide 14: `AFR` — Which Peripheral Gets the Pin?
sections.body:
**MODER** uses 00 input,01 output,10 alternate,11 analog per pin. GPIOA reset 0xEBFFFFFF is analog except PA13/14 SWD. Analog disables digital input: IDR reads 0 regardless of button level. Explicitly select input before interpreting presses.

A **transistor** is an electronic switch: P-MOS connects toward supply; N-MOS toward ground.

**OTYPER**0=push-pull,1=open-drain. **Push-pull** alternates P-MOS high/N-MOS low; opposing outputs can short 3.3 V to ground. **Open-drain** uses only N-MOS low or release, with a pull-up making high. Shared outputs form **wired-AND** (any low wins); I2C requires it. Here OTYPER stays 0.

**OSPEEDR**00/01/10/11=very-low/low/high/very-high edge slew, not toggle frequency. Fast edges increase noise/current. Reset 0C000000 gives PA13 very-high, others very-low; LEDs retain slow slew.

PUPDR 00=no pull, 01=up, 10=down, 11=reserved. Reset 24000000 gives PA13 up and PA14 down; other pins float. Pull-ups onPA0/1 produce 24000005. A floating released button can report phantom presses. Grounded buttons read 0 pressed, 1 released; button_down returns pin_read()==0.

IDR is read-only and measures actual voltage, even for output pins; ODR is the requested drive level. `(GPIOA->IDR >> 1)&1u` extractsPA1. For 0x0000A001 onlyPA15, PA13, PA0 are high, soPA1 is 0.

Alternate mode also needs AFR selection. Four-bit nibbles choose per-pin functions from the datasheet; PA2/PA3 AF1 create AFR[0]=0x00001100. AFR[1] maps pins8–15 from low nibble to high. Wrong AF can leave a running device disconnected from its pin.

sections.body:
Enable RCC IOPENR GPIOAEN/GPIOBEN, configure mode/pull/type/speed, then data. Unclocked ports may ignore writes/read 0. Replace a two-bit **field** while preserving others:

```c
port->MODER = (port->MODER & ~(3u << (pin*2u))) | (mode << (pin*2u));
port->PUPDR = (port->PUPDR & ~(3u << (pin*2u))) | (pull << (pin*2u));
```
Locate both bits, clear them, insert the value. PA5 uses 11:10; setting 10 alone cannot clear 11.

PA5’s shift 10 gives mask 0xC00, inverse 0xFFFFF3FF. ResetEBFFFFFF &inverse=0xEBFFF3FF; insert output 1<<10=400 yieldsEBFFF7FF. OR alone cannot turn analog 11 intooutput01. Direct assignment 400 would clear all other fields, including SWD.

| Step | MODER |
|---|---|
|Reset|0xEBFFFFFF|
|PA5 output|0xEBFFF7FF|
|PA0 input|0xEBFFF7FC|
|PA1 input|0xEBFFF7F0|
|PA2/PA3 alternate|0xEBFFF7A0|

Reading the final low fields gives pin 7analog, 6analog, 5output, 4analog, 3AF, 2AF, 1input, 0input. PUPDR follows 24000000→24000001→24000005 forPA0/1 pull-ups. The same clear/insert shape works for all two-bit-per-pin registers, and the banner can decode the result back into per-pin settings.

sections.body:
Route: port selection → edge detection/latch → EXTI unmask → NVIC enable/priority → vector. A **latch** remembers an event; **unmask** allows delivery; **IRQ** is an external request number. Pending does not guarantee entry. EXTI base 0x40021800; NVIC0xE000E100.

|Block|Offset|Register and role|
|---|---|---|
|EXTI|00/04|RTSR1/FTSR1 rising/falling enables|
|EXTI|08|SWIER1 software edge request|
|EXTI|0C/10|RPR1/FPR1 separate rising/falling latches; write1 clears|
|EXTI|14–5C|Reserved|
|EXTI|60/64/68/6C|EXTICR[0–3] port selections|
|EXTI|70–7C|Reserved|
|EXTI|80/84|IMR1 interrupt mask /EMR1 event mask|
|NVIC|000/080|ISER/ICER enable/disable commands|
|NVIC|100/180|ISPR/ICPR set/clear pending|
|NVIC|300–31C|IPR[0–7] priority bytes|

Line n watches pin n on one port. EXTICR[n/4] assigns byte8(n mod 4)+7:8(n mod 4), with a low three-bit port code; rest reserved. A=0,B=1,C=2,D=3,F=5. PA1: EXTICR0 byte15:8=0; PC13: EXTICR3 byte15:8=2, value 0x200. PA1/PB1 cannot share line 1; PC1 is unexposed despite codeC. PortA matches reset 0; relocating requires explicit selection. C0 uses EXTI, F4 SYSCFG.

```c
uint32_t shift=(line%4u)*8u;
EXTI->EXTICR[line/4u] = (EXTI->EXTICR[line/4u] & ~(0xFFu<<shift))
                         | (port_code<<shift);
EXTI->RTSR1 |= 2u;
EXTI->FTSR1 |= 2u;
EXTI->RPR1 = 2u;
EXTI->FPR1 = 2u;
EXTI->IMR1 |= 2u;
NVIC_SetPriority(EXTI0_1_IRQn,2);
NVIC_EnableIRQ(EXTI0_1_IRQn);
```
Line 1 is bit 1=2 in edge/latch/mask registers. Clear pending before unmasking. IMR includes GPIO 0–15 plus direct 19/23/25/31; EMR also includes 16–18. SWIER fakes an edge; RPR/FPR vary as hardware sets and handler clears. PRIMASK0=0 permits configurable interrupts after reset.

IRQ 5 groups EXTI0/1; IRQ 6 groups 2/3; IRQ 7 groups 4–15. C031 uses external IRQ 0–28; core supports up to 32. ISER writes 1<<5=0x20; writingzero leaves other enables alone. Priority 2 becomes byte 0x80: IRQ 5 is IPR1 byte 1, givingword 0x00008000; only top 2 bits of each byte exist, with 0 most urgent.

Vector 16+5=21 sits at 0x08000000+21×4=0x08000054. This build’s bytes 3D020008 mean tagged 0x0800023D; nm gives EXTI0_1_IRQHandler code at 0x0800023C. Pending bits identify which member of a shared vector caused entry.

CMSIS names used while tracing the path include EXTI->EXTICR, EXTI->RTSR1, EXTI->FTSR1, EXTI->IMR1, EXTI->SWIER1 and NVIC->ISPR. GPIO reads use GPIOA->IDR; mode/pull setup uses GPIOA->MODER and GPIOA->PUPDR. Output requests can use GPIOA->ODR or GPIOA->BRR. IRQ 4/5/6/7 occupy priority fields 7:6, 15:14, 23:22, 31:30 of NVIC->IPR[1].

Add each hexadecimal table offset to the block base for its address.

EXTICR[0] names its port-select fields EXTI0 bits 2:0, EXTI1 bits 10:8, EXTI2 bits 18:16 and EXTI3 bits 26:24 within the four allocated bytes. IMR1.IM1 is bit 1; PRIMASK.PM is bit 0. The remaining bits of each EXTICR byte are reserved.

sections.body:
Source predictions: bounce enabled/1 kHz polling gives A one, sometimes 2–3 sampled changes; B tens of edges. Without bounce, each sees one per press/release. Record observations; simulator behavior/timing may differ.

Separate **detection**, **delivery** and **handling**: a flag can exist with delivery disabled; entry alone does not prove correct acknowledgement.

Silent-input checklist:

1. Clock missing: writes can vanish.
2. Input mode missing: analog mode leaves digital reads at zero.
3. Pull missing: an undriven input can report phantom presses.
4. Wrong EXTICR: EXTI watches another port.
5. IMR masked: the edge may be pending but cannot reach interrupt delivery.
6. NVIC disabled: a request waits without handler entry.
7. Handler name wrong: the vector still reaches Default_Handler.
8. Source latch uncleared: repeated entry prevents main from progressing.

Debugger interactions can distort observations: a click includes press/release while halted simulation freezes time, a breakpoint on b_edges++ stops for every bounce, and debounce_step’s first line is visited 1000 times/s. Latch a button with Ctrl-click or hold A/B; break at accepted state (`d->stable=raw`) or b_count++.

```
-exec set *(unsigned int *)0x40021808 = 2
-exec set *(unsigned int *)0xE000E200 = 32
```
First writes EXTI SWIER1 and is predicted to set a rising latch on line 1, so the handler counts an edge. Second writes NVIC ISPR to pendIRQ5 without an EXTI latch, so a correct handler counts nothing. The source labels GDB acceptance/these outcomes as unobserved predictions, requiring verification.

GPIO field arithmetic, single-store commands and the pending/NVIC/vector route transfer to other peripherals. This lesson’s timebase still polls COUNTFLAG, which remembers one wrap: a 5 ms printf can lose four ticks and make ms_now slow. The next lesson turns wrap events into SysTick interrupts.

sections.title: Timer map, fields and frequency
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: The Timer — Every Register on One Page
Slide 5b: A Timer Is a Counter With Three Registers
sections.body:
A **timer** counts pulses: **PSC** divides clock, **CNT** is current count, **ARR** ends the period, **CCR1** compares/captures. First derive tick duration. TIM3 base 0x40000400; TIM14 base 0x40002000; matching offsets, fewer TIM14 features. Both are 16-bit. A **field** groups setting bits; **preload** buffers a setting until update.

|Offset|Register|Purpose / use|
|---|---|---|
|00|CR1|CEN run, ARPE preload|
|04|CR2|Master mode/trigger output|
|08|SMCR|Slave clock/trigger mode|
|0C|DIER|UIE update/CC1IE capture IRQ enable|
|10|SR|UIF update/CC1IF capture flags|
|14|EGR|UG force update|
|18|CCMR1|Channels1/2 output or input layout|
|1C|CCMR2|Channels3/4|
|20|CCER|Channel enable/polarity|
|24|CNT|Live count; trigger stopwatch|
|28|PSC|Clock divider minus1|
|2C|ARR|Period count minus1|
|30|RCR|Advanced repetition|
|34/38/3C/40|CCR1/2/3/4|Compare or capture values|
|44–68|BDTR, DCR, DMAR, CCMR3, CCR5, CCR6, AF1, AF2, TISEL|Advanced outputs, DMA/input-selection features|

Register groups: PSC/ARR/CNT=timebase; EGR/DIER/SR=generate/enable/report events; CCMR1/CCER/CCR1=interpret/enable/data; CR1=run. **Output compare** tests count against a value; **input capture** saves count at an edge; **DMA requests** ask hardware to move data.

The nine principal controls combine timebase PSC/ARR/CNT, eventsEGR/DIER/SR, channelCCMR1/CCER/CCR1 and CR1. Fields:CR1 UIFREMAP bit 11, CKD bits 9:8, ARPE bit 7, CMS bits 6:5, DIR bit 4, OPM bit 3, URS bit 2, UDIS bit 1, CEN bit 0; PSC/ARR/CCR1 use 15:0. CNT uses 15:0 with UIFCPY31 when remapping is enabled. EGR hasTG6, CC1G1, UG0; DIER UDE bit 8, TIE bit 6, CC1IE1, UIE bit 0; SR CC1OF9, TIF bit 6, CC1IF1, UIF bit 0. CCER CC1NP3, CC1NE2, CC1P1, CC1E0. CCMR1 output hasOC1M extension 16, OC1M bits 6:4, OC1PE3, OC1FE2, CC1S bits 1:0; input hasIC1F bits 7:4, IC1PSC bits 3:2, CC1S bits 1:0. CC1S decides the interpretation. Header 32-bit masks also serve other STM32 timers and do not make these counters 32-bit.

Frequency equations:
`f_count = f_timer/(PSC+1)`
`f_update = f_timer/((PSC+1)(ARR+1))`
At 48 MHz, PSC 47=0x002F gives 1 MHz, one count/µs. ARR19999=0x4E1F gives 20000 counts=20 ms=50 Hz. TIM14 uses PSC 47, ARR 0xFFFF for a 65536 µs wrap. Mistaken PSC 48 gives 48000000/(49×20000)=48.98 Hz. Both divider registers encode N-1 because counting includeszero.

Add each hexadecimal table offset to the block base for its address.

The fourth output-mode bit is explicitly named OC1M_3 at CCMR1 bit 16, separated from OC1M bits 6:4. PWM mode 1 has the complete field 0110, so OC1M_3=0 and bits 6:4=110.

sections.title: Capture timestamps and the simulator fallback
sourceHeadings: Slide 12: Input Capture — the Hardware Takes the Timestamp
Slide 13: Measuring the Echo
Slide 13b: What Wokwi Showed — No Capture, So EXTI
Slide 14: Two Variables From One Interrupt — Tearing
sections.body:
**Input capture** copies CNT into CCR1 at the edge, before requesting an ISR. Handler delay changes read time, not timestamp. EXTI reading live CNT timestamps handler arrival; unequal edge delays distort width.

Rising begins echo, falling ends it. **Round-trip time** includes travel out and back. Subtract timestamps, then scale width to distance; a 16-bit cast keeps subtraction modulo 65536.

HC-SR04 uses a 10 µs trigger and echo round-trip width, nominal 58 µs/cm in the cited part documentation. TIM14 counts at 1 MHz. CCMR1=1 selectsCC1S01/TI1 input; CCER=0xB setsCC1NP3, CC1P1, CC1E0 to capture both edges. EnableDIER CC1IE. The ISR readsuint16_t CCR1 (clearingCC1IF), identifies current pin state, records rising time or computes `(uint16_t)(fall-rise)`. Width remains valid across one 16-bit wrap:65536 µs≈65.5 ms, longer than 400 cm×58=23200 µs. CNT also times the 10 µs trigger. Reading a capture register is a third flag-clear convention; consult its documented sequence.

Wokwi observation on 2026-10-04 producedecho0 us/0 cm because timer input capture was unimplemented: the board model’s timer support was PWM-oriented. Firmware therefore also listens to both PA7 EXTI edges and reads TIM14 CNT in EXTI4_15_IRQHandler, clearingRPR/FPR with mask assignments. Prefer capture when it has delivered a pulse, else use EXTI, and report the source/counts.

Measured Wokwi line:
```
t=9000 ms  TIM3 50/s  echo 5882 us =101 cm (EXTI)
servo1495 us  edges cap0 exti161
```
Capture remained 0; EXTI grew 20 edges/s for 10 pings/s. Slider 100 cm produced 5882 µs≈58.8 µs/cm (sound 340m/s), and integerdivision by 58 reported 101 cm. Mapping gives 2000-101×1000/200=1495 µs; bar uses(200-101)×8/200=3 LEDs. Equal latency on both edges approximately cancels, yielding a width within a microsecond or two in that observation; a delayed single edge destroys that assumption. Silicon capture remains the reliable method.

When ISR publishes echo_count and echo_us, individually atomic reads can still combine generations. Copy them within a short critical section, preservingPRIMASK when necessary. Hardware capture remains timely while its ISR waits pending, provided CCR1 is read before a newer edge overwrites it. EXTI fallback timestamps do not have that protection.

Consistent pair copy:```c
uint32_t saved = __get_PRIMASK();
__disable_irq();
uint32_t n = echo_count;
uint32_t us = echo_us;
__set_PRIMASK(saved);
```
The copy prevents mixing a new count with a preceding pulse width. It does not make EXTI timestamps independent of latency.

sections.title: Priorities, cross-checks and timer lab failures
sourceHeadings: Slide 15: Three Interrupts, Three Priorities
Slide 16: Two Clocks Checking Each Other
Slide 17: The Silent-Failure Checklist, Timer Edition
Slide 18: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
A **deadline** is latest successful service time. Capture priority 1 must read before CCR1 is overwritten; TIM3 priority 2 has 20 ms frames. SysTick priority 3 is lowest but must run before multiple ticks coalesce.

NVIC IPR4 covers IRQs 16–19. Value 0x40000080 sets TIM3 IRQ 16 priority 2 at bits 7:6 and TIM14 IRQ 19 priority 1 at bits 31:30. SCB SHPR3=0xC0000000 sets SysTick priority 3 at bits 31:30; PendSV uses 23:22. More urgent handlers preempt less urgent ones. Equals wait; simultaneous equals use the lower IRQ number first. Deadline-monotonic orders by deadline. Rate-monotonic orders by period, matching when deadlines equal periods.

A **cross-check** compares timer updates with software milliseconds. Disagreement can expose firmware or simulator clock errors; a plausible report alone is not measurement.

Cross-check TIM3 updates against SysTick seconds. The sample reportt 5000 ms, TIM3 50/s, echo 5800 µs=100 cm, servo 1500 µs, last line 8 ms describes expected arithmetic/reporting. About 88 characters×86.8 µs=7.64 ms explains printing cost; interrupt timekeeping continues normally through it.

Evidence distinction:50/s was measured in Renode after correcting its timer configuration. Its initial platform timer clock 10 MHz yielded 10/s rather than expected 50/s, exposing an instrument mismatch. The source labels that specific cross-check as not yet watched in Wokwi, although the later Wokwi fallback line independently reported 50/s. A Wokwi took=0 can reflect accelerated UART modeling rather than zero hardware transmission time.

| Lab/check failure | Consequence |
|---|---|
|MissingAPBENR1/2 timer gate|Registers0, no count|
|Missing UG|First period uses old divisor|
|PSC 48 instead47|About2% slow; compare updates/s|
|Writing1 to clear UIF|Continuous handler re-entry|
|WrongAF or missingCC1E|Timer runs but pin has no PWM|
|Only rising captures|No pulse widths|
|Wronghandler name|Default vector remains installed|

Readback banner checks PSC/ARR/computedrate, AF fields, polarity and installed handlers. Lab also measures servo endpoints and deliberately changesAF. Timers generalize:TIM3 generates a waveform, TIM14 measures one, TIM1/16/17 share the model with different features. Use elapsed-time differences; keep cooperative jobs short. The next scheduler lesson lets one job be interrupted for another.
